result: Late-life depression is underdiagnosed and undertreated due to misconceptions about depression being a normal part of aging among patients, general practitioners, and older adults themselves, leading to misattribution of symptoms and reluctance to seek help.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6 are all supported by citations to peer-reviewed literature (Park and Unützer 2011; Allan et al. 2014; Nair et al. 2020) and collectively establish the problem of underdiagnosis and undertreatment of LLD. These are well-documented phenomena in the field and the citations appear appropriate.

result: Late-life depression has serious consequences including a chronic-remitting course, increased suicide risk, decreased functioning across multiple domains, increased mortality, and higher healthcare costs.
evaluation: Claims C7-C10 are supported by citations to Blazer 2003 and Bock et al. 2017. These represent well-established clinical characteristics of LLD documented in the literature. The claims are appropriately cited and represent consensus knowledge in the field.

result: Research on late-life depression has emphasized biological changes while psychocognitive etiological theories remain limited.
evaluation: Claims C11-C12 are supported by appropriate citations and accurately characterize the state of the field. This observation sets up the rationale for the authors' theoretical contribution and is well-documented in the cited literature.

result: Emotionally healthy aging is linked to successful adaptation to age-related limitations that become evident from midlife onward, making midlife a pivotal phase for well-being. Longitudinal studies support that midlife functioning predicts later mood and depression, suggesting some individuals who develop late-life depression may have failed to successfully adapt during earlier life stages.
evaluation: Claims C13-C17 are well-supported by multiple citations to established literature (Carstensen 2006; Park and Reuter-Lorenz 2009; Brassen et al. 2012; Mather 2016; Heckhausen et al. 2019; Lachman et al. 2015; Dennerstein et al. 2004; Campbell et al. 2020; Richmond-Rakerd et al. 2021). The inference in C17 is reasonable given the longitudinal evidence cited, though it represents a hypothesis that requires further testing.

result: Late-life depression shows considerable heterogeneity in neuroanatomical, cognitive, clinical, and genetic profiles. Late-onset depression (onset ≥60 years) differs from early-onset depression in clinical features including absence of family history, presence of cognitive deficits, more somatic symptoms, and less personality dysfunction.
evaluation: Claims C18-C23 are supported by appropriate citations (Wen et al. 2022; Fiske et al. 2009; Naismith et al. 2012). The characterization of LLD heterogeneity and the distinction between late-onset and early-onset depression are well-established in the literature. C19 appropriately notes the variability in age cutoffs used in the field.

result: Early-onset depression may promote later vascular depression through effects on vascular health, inflammation, and epigenetics. Some late-life depression subgroups likely arise in midlife and are associated with cognitive deficits that may lead to clinical symptoms later in life.
evaluation: Claims C24-C26 are supported by citations to Alexopoulos 2019, Moura et al. 2019, and Sierra et al. 2004. The causal inference in C26 about cognitive deficits 'paving the way' for later symptoms is appropriately qualified as a possibility rather than established fact. These claims represent current understanding in the field.

result: The most striking neurobiological feature of late-life depression is disruption of fronto-subcortical structure, including networks involving dlPFC, vmPFC, ACC, basal ganglia, amygdala, and hippocampus. Meta-analysis shows the most consistent decline in ACC and medial PFC, with late-onset LLD particularly involving frontoparietal control, dorsal attention, and visual networks. Multiple etiological factors contribute including vascular mechanisms, inflammation, neuroimmune dysfunction, neurodegeneration, and amyloid accumulation.
evaluation: Claims C27-C31 are well-supported by comprehensive reviews (Naismith et al. 2012; Kim and Han 2021) and a meta-analysis of 17 structural imaging studies (Zhukovsky et al. 2021). The etiological factors are supported by recent reviews (Alexopoulos 2019; Jellinger 2022). This represents a solid synthesis of current neurobiological understanding of LLD.

result: White matter lesions (WMLs) are a highly consistent finding in late-life depression, caused predominantly by ischemic changes in small vessels and localized mainly in subcortical structures and frontal projections. WML burden directly relates to symptom severity and reduced cognitive control in LLD patients as well as nondepressed older and middle-aged individuals. WMLs are associated with elevated sgACC BOLD response during affective tasks, predict incident depression over time, can occur as early as the mid-40s, and represent a strong risk factor for LLD.
evaluation: Claims C32-C43 are extensively supported by multiple citations (van Agtmaal et al. 2017; Geraets et al. 2022; Alexopoulos et al. 1997; Taylor et al. 2003; Kim and Han 2021; Köhler et al. 2010; Mayda et al. 2011; Sierra et al. 2004; Aizenstein et al. 2011; van Sloten et al. 2015; Moura et al. 2019). The vascular depression hypothesis is well-established. The inference in C43 that WMLs are a 'strong risk factor' is reasonable given the predictive and early-onset evidence cited.

result: Patients with late-life depression show severe deficits in executive functions (cognitive flexibility, planning, response-inhibition, set-shifting) as well as processing speed, learning, and memory. These cognitive deficits are associated with problematic prognosis and clinical outcomes.
evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by appropriate citations (Herrmann et al. 2007; Naismith et al. 2012; Alexopoulos et al. 2002; Alexopoulos 2019). The characterization of cognitive deficits in LLD and their clinical significance is well-established in the literature and led to the conceptualization of 'depression executive dysfunction syndrome.'

result: Despite the involvement of prefrontal regions in emotion regulation, surprisingly few studies have focused on emotional processing in late-life depression. Existing behavioral findings suggest a cognitive bias toward negativity, and fMRI studies show neural changes in dlPFC, vmPFC, ACC, and amygdala-hippocampus complex in response to emotional inputs, suggesting dysfunctions in emotion regulation particularly for negative stimuli.
evaluation: Claims C47-C50 are supported by multiple citations (Ochsner et al. 2012; Etkin et al. 2015; Broomfield et al. 2007; Brassen et al. 2008, 2012; Aizenstein et al. 2011; Huang et al. 2019; Baruch et al. 2021; Briceño et al. 2015; Wong et al. 2016; Leal et al. 2017; Vasudev et al. 2018). The observation about limited research (C47) is appropriate and the inference about emotion regulation dysfunction (C50) is reasonable given the neural changes documented.

result: Patients with late-life depression show heightened behavioral and autonomic regret responsiveness to missed opportunities compared to healthy older adults, paralleled by reduced vmPFC engagement. In contrast, emotionally healthy older adults show reduced regret responsiveness compared to both LLD patients and healthy young adults, associated with increased vmPFC engagement that may help overcome regretful thoughts.
evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are all supported by citations to Brassen et al. 2012 and related work (Suri and Gross 2012; Aldao et al. 2010). The findings represent specific experimental evidence for differential emotion regulation in LLD versus healthy aging. The inference in C55 about vmPFC helping to overcome regretful thoughts is appropriately qualified as 'may help' and is supported by the cited evidence.

result: Late-life depression is the most common mental disorder in later life, yet three out of four older adults describe themselves as having aged successfully. Epidemiological data show older people report better emotional well-being than younger adults, even during the COVID-19 pandemic, representing a 'paradox of aging.'
evaluation: Claims C56-C59 are supported by appropriate citations (Volkert et al. 2013; Bowling and Dieppe 2005; Stone et al. 2010; Blanchflower 2021; Carstensen et al. 2020). These claims establish the paradox that motivates the investigation of successful aging mechanisms. The evidence is from large epidemiological studies and is well-established.

result: Three major lifespan theories explain successful aging: (1) the SOC model emphasizes selection, optimization, and compensation in goal pursuit; (2) the motivational theory of lifespan development emphasizes maximizing personal agency through primary control (goal selection, engagement, disengagement) and secondary control strategies; (3) socioemotional selectivity theory focuses on how remaining lifetime perception drives shifts toward present-focused, emotionally meaningful goals. All three theories highlight the need to adapt to limited resources in goal setting and pursuit, with older people selecting emotion regulation strategies based on available resources.
evaluation: Claims C60-C67 are supported by appropriate citations to foundational work (Baltes and Baltes 1990; Heckhausen et al. 2010, 2019; Carstensen 2006; Urry and Gross 2010). These represent well-established theoretical frameworks in the field. The synthesis in C66 is a reasonable inference from the three theories described. This provides important theoretical context for the authors' model.

result: The most consistent finding in emotionally healthy aging is a positivity effect—increased processing of positive or decreased processing of negative information in older versus younger adults, documented across attention, memory, and decision-making. Meta-analysis of over 100 studies shows mean age distances of 45-55 years between groups, with effect size scaling with age distance, suggesting gradual lifespan changes. The positivity effect is associated with increased emotional stability and better immune function.
evaluation: Claims C68-C73 are well-supported by citations to comprehensive reviews and meta-analyses (Reed et al. 2014; Mather 2016; Brassen et al. 2011; Kalokerinos et al. 2014). The inference in C71 about gradual changes is reasonable given the scaling relationship. This represents a well-established phenomenon in the successful aging literature.

result: Emotionally healthy older people engage differently in emotion regulation compared to younger and depressed older adults, potentially becoming better at regulating emotions. They are more effective at situation selection (e.g., narrowing social networks), deploy more attention to positive information to improve and stabilize mood, are more effective at focusing away from negative emotions, and perceive downregulating negative emotions as less costly. However, they are less successful at cognitively demanding reappraisal. This shift from explicit, cognitively demanding toward less costly, attentional, implicit regulation likely results from reduced cognitive capacity and may reflect successful SOC adaptation. Age effects on emotion regulation have not been consistently observed, but evidence points toward differences in effectiveness and frequency of strategy use.
evaluation: Claims C74-C87 are extensively supported by multiple citations (Gross et al. 1997; Nolen-Hoeksema and Aldao 2011; Isaacowitz 2022; Brassen et al. 2012; Urry and Gross 2010; Gross 1998; English and Carstensen 2014; Isaacowitz et al. 2008; Brassen et al. 2011; Phillips et al. 2008; Scheibe and Blanchard-Fields 2009; Shiota and Levenson 2009; Opitz et al. 2012; Eldesouky and English 2018; Livingstone and Isaacowitz 2019). The inference about reduced cognitive capacity (C84) and SOC adaptation (C85) is appropriately qualified. The acknowledgment of inconsistent findings (C86) is important for balanced evaluation.

result: Neuroimaging findings indicate a key role of vmPFC/ACC in emotion regulation during successful aging. The vmPFC integrates contextual information, goals, motivational states, and learning history to compute subjective value and orchestrate responses, with input from subcortical regions (amygdala, ventral striatum) about affective relevance and lateral PFC representing current goals. vmPFC-amygdala coupling predicts positivity bias in memory, increased ACC/vmPFC activity occurs during selective focus on positive information (related to emotional well-being), and increased vmPFC activation to negative information associates with enhanced striatal and reduced amygdala signaling. The vmPFC may functionally compensate for dlPFC decline in healthy aging, as lateral PFC undergoes strong age-related decline while vmPFC structure and function remain relatively preserved. Increased vmPFC activity to negative stimuli correlates with lower lateral PFC function/structure in healthy older adults, and pronounced vmPFC engagement may reflect a shift toward implicit emotion regulation.
evaluation: Claims C88-C103 are extensively supported by multiple citations (Isaacowitz 2022; Sakaki et al. 2013; Leclerc and Kensinger 2008; Brassen et al. 2011, 2012; Corbett et al. 2020; Roy et al. 2012; Haber and Knutson 2010; Lapate et al. 2022; Mather 2016; Fjell et al. 2009; van Reekum et al. 2018; Suri and Gross 2012). The compensatory hypothesis (C99) and implicit regulation hypothesis (C103) are appropriately qualified as speculation. This represents a comprehensive synthesis of neuroimaging evidence for vmPFC's role in successful aging.

result: Most studies demonstrating the positivity effect have not provided explicit emotion regulation instructions, and findings could be attributed to attentional bias. Studies with cognitive manipulation support the relevance of cognitive resources for top-down regulation—the attentional positivity effect in older adults occurred only with more attentional resources available, and focusing on positive/ignoring negative information related to executive control function. However, studies on early processes and habituation suggest bottom-up processes are also involved. Most likely, both implicit and explicit processes orchestrate age-related emotional adaptation as a function of neurocognitive resources, compensatory abilities, and lifelong learning.
evaluation: Claims C104-C110 are supported by multiple citations (Mather and Carstensen 2003; Isaacowitz et al. 2008; Brassen et al. 2011, 2012; Kryla-Lighthall and Mather 2009; Mather 2012; Sasse et al. 2014; Gronchi et al. 2018; Petro et al. 2021). The synthesis in C110 is a reasonable inference that acknowledges the complexity of the evidence. This represents a balanced evaluation of the implicit versus explicit debate in the field.

result: Goal selection and pursuit rely on habitual and flexible control. In emotional contexts, individuals habitually seek to avoid negative and approach positive situations, but need flexible strategies depending on situation and resources. Implicit processes can be involved in all emotion regulation stages (goal selection, monitoring, regulation selection, enactment). Goals may be consciously adopted then implicitly activated by context; monitoring divergences from goals may occur implicitly (related to vmPFC/ventral ACC); habitual strategies formed by frequent use can be automatically elicited; and implicit regulation may bias attention toward goal-supportive stimuli (associated with vmPFC/ACC activation). Implicit regulation may be less cognitively demanding but at the cost of flexibility. Cognitive flexibility is a major component of cognitive control involving lateral PFC and OFC. Explicit emotion regulation depends on cost-benefit analysis—engaging costly strategies when benefits outweigh costs—which relies on prefrontal function, particularly dorso- and ventrolateral PFC. Given age-related changes in dorsolateral PFC, how and when people engage in cost-benefit trade-offs likely changes across the lifespan. Older adults show increased perceived cognitive costs reducing motivation for demanding activities, but when motivation is high and tasks manageable, they can still selectively invest cognitive resources in costly decision-making.
evaluation: Claims C111-C126 are extensively supported by appropriate citations (Cushman and Morris 2015; Raio et al. 2016; Koole et al. 2015; Williams et al. 2009; Etkin et al. 2006, 2015; Egner et al. 2008; Christou-Champi et al. 2015; Vogt et al. 2011; Brassen et al. 2011; Reed et al. 2014; Sasse et al. 2014; Quirk et al. 2006; Friedman and Robbins 2022; Buhle et al. 2014; Kool et al. 2018; Smittenaar et al. 2013; Cortese 2022; Fjell et al. 2009; Cabeza and Dennis 2013; Hess et al. 2016; Devine et al. 2021; Ruel et al. 2021). The inference in C124 is reasonable given the cited evidence on PFC changes. This provides important theoretical framework from cognitive neuroscience for understanding emotion regulation across the lifespan.

result: Neurobehavioral findings in successful aging suggest a shift in balance from flexible to implicit habitual control in the second half of life. Adaptation in self-control is a lifelong process but probably particularly critical in midlife, as it is a phase of fundamental changes and individuals are still capable of building aging preparedness.
evaluation: Claims C127-C128 represent reasonable inferences from the extensive evidence reviewed in prior sections. C127 synthesizes the neurobehavioral findings appropriately. C128 is supported by citations to Lachman et al. 2015 and Richmond-Rakerd et al. 2021. These claims set up the focus on midlife as a critical period.

result: Large cross-sectional epidemiological surveys consistently show a U-shaped pattern of subjective well-being with a nadir around age 50, corresponding to peak unhappiness in the late 40s across Europe and the United States. This U-shape has been observed in over 140 countries and holds regardless of sociodemographic covariates or cohort effects. Midlife is considered a critical period for preparing for aging demands, but factors mediating well-being in middle years are less well understood than earlier/later stages, and it is unknown whether the midlife low point predicts later mood. Discussed mediators include approaching physical, cognitive, and socioeconomic demands, age discrimination, financial pressures, limited opportunities, and changing family dynamics.
evaluation: Claims C129-C136 are supported by multiple citations to large epidemiological studies (Blanchflower 2020, 2021; Blanchflower and Oswald 2008; Stone et al. 2010; Kaiser et al. 2022; Richmond-Rakerd et al. 2021; Lachman et al. 2015). The acknowledgment of gaps in knowledge (C134, C135) is appropriate. This establishes the empirical basis for focusing on midlife as a critical period.

result: White matter integrity of prefrontal-subcortical connections starts to degenerate significantly between ages 40-50, potentially accelerated by WMLs that first peak in the mid-40s and are already associated with cognitive decline. WML occurrence may be driven by cardiovascular dysfunctions or inflammatory processes associated with metabolic diseases becoming more prevalent in midlife. Gray matter changes relate to cognitive decline in executive functions observable as early as age 40. Cognitive abilities are most important for successful adaptation; deficits in cognitive control relate to maladaptive emotion-regulation strategies and increase vulnerability for first-onset depression. Cognitive capacity is relevant for both using cognitively demanding strategies and flexibly selecting adequate strategies given changing resources. Long-established regulation strategies may no longer be sufficiently usable due to decreased resources. Adequate stress regulation may be compromised by hormonal changes with potential neuronal consequences. The increasing awareness of aging mind/body, limited opportunities, and decreasing time horizon may be particularly crucial for well-being as people in midlife review their 'first half' of life. Perceiving low controllability to cope with missed opportunities can severely impact self-efficacy, agency, and well-being now and later.
evaluation: Claims C137-C152 are extensively supported by multiple citations (Gunning-Dixon et al. 2009; Yeatman et al. 2014; Moura et al. 2019; d'Arbeloff et al. 2019; Power et al. 2017; Mattson and Arumugam 2018; Ferreira et al. 2014; Park and Festini 2016; Singh-Manoux et al. 2012; Ferguson et al. 2021; Cañas et al. 2003; Joormann and Gotlib 2010; Gotlib and Joormann 2010; Urry and Gross 2010; Heckhausen et al. 2019; Hodes and Epperson 2019; Kiesow et al. 2021; Carstensen 2006; Ingersoll-Dayton et al. 2010; Lachman et al. 2015; Robinson and Lachman 2017; Blazer 2002; Wrosch and Heckhausen 2002). This comprehensively documents the neurobiological and psychological challenges emerging in midlife that may compromise adaptation.

result: A longitudinal study following a cohort from birth to age 45 found that not only childhood self-control but also self-control in midlife was associated with pace of aging and preparedness to manage later-life health, financial, and social demands, even after accounting for childhood factors. This indicates self-control in midlife is a malleable target for intervention but may also be a target for disruption.
evaluation: Claims C153-C154 are based on a specific longitudinal study and supported by citation to Richmond-Rakerd et al. 2021. The inference in C154 about malleability is reasonable given the longitudinal evidence. This provides important empirical support for the focus on midlife self-control as a modifiable factor.

result: Longitudinal studies (mostly in women) show that negative mood, negative attitudes toward aging, affective instability, chronic stress, and less optimism in nondepressed midlife adults predict later depression. Lower positive mood and higher stress at age 50 is associated with higher depressive symptoms at age 70, suggesting higher positive mood and effective stress regulation during the midlife-to-late-life transition may be a resilience factor for emotional health in aging.
evaluation: Claims C155-C157 are supported by citations to longitudinal studies (Dennerstein et al. 2004; Lachman et al. 2015; Campbell et al. 2020). The inference in C157 about resilience factors is reasonable given the predictive associations documented. The limitation to mostly female samples is appropriately noted. This provides direct empirical evidence linking midlife factors to later depression.

result: Dysthymic disorder can persist from midlife into late life, and midlife mood disturbance has predictive value for later inflammation, which is a strong risk factor for late-life depression.
evaluation: Claims C158-C159 are supported by citations to Blazer 2003 and Alexopoulos 2019. These represent established pathways linking midlife mood disturbance to later depression risk through both persistence and inflammatory mechanisms.

result: There is striking overlap in neurobehavioral factors involved in emotionally healthy aging and late-life depression. Healthy aging shows a positivity effect while LLD shows negativity bias. The positivity effect is reflected in vmPFC/ventral ACC engagement, which is functionally altered in LLD patients. vmPFC structure is relatively preserved in healthy aging but shows structural and functional disruption in LLD. Higher-order cognitive functions are involved in developing the positivity effect and are needed for flexibly dealing with challenges, while executive functions and dlPFC are strongly affected in LLD. Figure 2 provides an overview of prefrontal regions critical for emotionally successful aging and LLD.
evaluation: Claims C160-C169 synthesize the extensive evidence reviewed in prior sections and are supported by appropriate citations (Reed et al. 2014; Broomfield et al. 2007; Brassen et al. 2011, 2008, 2012; Mather 2016; Aizenstein et al. 2011; Fjell et al. 2009; Naismith et al. 2012; Zhukovsky et al. 2021; Fischer et al. 2010; Mather and Knight 2005; Murty et al. 2009; Ritchey et al. 2011; Roalf et al. 2011; Sasse et al. 2014; Friedman and Robbins 2022; Alexopoulos 2019). The inference about overlap (C160) is reasonable and well-supported. Figure 2 provides visual summary of the evidence. This represents a key synthesis supporting the authors' model.

result: The authors propose a neurocognitive model of emotional adaptation in the second half of life. They hypothesize that some LLD patients have not adapted successfully in emotional goals and strategies as suggested by lifespan theories, and that individuals who missed resource-adapted change in emotion regulation during midlife are at increased risk for later depression. The model proposes that in midlife, when people confront endings, limited opportunities, and aging, motivational goals shift toward prioritizing short-term, emotionally meaningful goals, leading to increased focus on pro-hedonic emotion regulation guided by implicit attentional bias. Successful adaptation depends on (i) lifelong acquired skills and vmPFC/ventral ACC networks mediating implicit habitual control, and (ii) sufficient resources for flexible strategy use when required (mediated by lateral PFC). The model proposes that one or both regulatory processes are impaired in at-risk individuals due to: (i) skill deficits, stress hypersensitivity, and preexisting cognitive bias; (ii) deficits in implicit learning/regulation due to medial PFC network disruption; or (iii) pronounced deficits in cognitive flexibility and lateral PFC networks. The model highlights a shift from flexible/explicit to habitual/implicit processes in healthy aging and suggests appropriate emotion regulation selection in midlife may be a promising intervention target. Figure 3 summarizes the model.
evaluation: Claims C170-C187 represent the authors' proposed theoretical model. While the model is grounded in the extensive evidence reviewed (as indicated by the SUPPORTED evaluations of prior claim groups), the model itself represents a novel theoretical synthesis that requires empirical testing. The claims are appropriately qualified as hypotheses, proposals, and postulates. The model makes testable predictions (e.g., C185 about transitions in decision-making) but these have not yet been tested. The model is logically coherent and integrates diverse evidence, but its core predictions about midlife adaptation as a critical factor in LLD risk require prospective longitudinal validation. The authors appropriately acknowledge this need for future research.

result: Figure 1 schematically illustrates that some individuals who develop depression at older ages may not have successfully used self-regulatory adaptation strategies at earlier ages.
evaluation: Claim C188 describes Figure 1, which provides a schematic illustration of the authors' hypothesis. The figure appropriately visualizes the concept that is supported by the longitudinal evidence cited (Richmond-Rakerd et al. 2021). This is a visual representation of the model's core hypothesis.
